periods.activity_title: Mapping the Population Machine: Demography's Three Components

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes on the board: 'A city's planners must decide how many new schools, hospitals, and water lines to build. What information do they need first?' Students write individual responses. Two or three are shared aloud. The teacher frames the unit: demography is the study of the features of a human population — its size, structure, composition, and how these change over time through births, deaths, and movement of people.

The teacher introduces and links the three components — size, structure and composition, and pattern and trend — with concrete examples: size tells you how many people; structure and composition tell you their age, sex, education, and occupation; pattern and trend show how these shift over time. Students receive a T-chart with two columns: 'Population Feature' and 'Why a Government or Business Needs It.' In pairs they fill in at least four rows — for instance, many children under 10 → more primary schools; a large working-age population (15–64) → employment-generation programmes; a large elderly share → more healthcare facilities; a growing young adult cohort → housing demand. The teacher circulates and probes: 'What is the working-age population? Which ages does it include and why does it matter to economic output?'

Pairs share their T-charts. The teacher uses responses to fix two key terms on the board with precise definitions: 'structure of population — how a population is made up on the basis of characteristics such as age, gender, and education' and 'working-age population — individuals between 15 and 64 years, the most productive in terms of economic output and workforce participation.' The class then discusses: if a neighbourhood has mostly elderly residents and few children, what services should the municipal council prioritise? Students must justify using the demography vocabulary introduced.

The teacher introduces the census as the official count of people living in a country at a particular time, conducted in India generally every ten years, gathering information on age, gender, marital status, education, languages, religion, family size, occupation, employment status, and income. Students write one paragraph explaining why a census is the foundation of demographic planning, using at least three data categories from this list and connecting each to one specific government decision — for example, 'If the census records a high number of children under 10 in a district, the government can plan new primary schools there.'

periods.section_context: Demography's three components, working-age population, census as planning tool
periods.teacher_notes: The T-chart activity is the analytical core of this unit: push students beyond listing facts to constructing the logic chain from population feature to government or business decision. A common confusion is treating 'structure' and 'size' as synonyms — draw a sharp contrast: size is a single number, structure is a profile of who those people are.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understand how population size and structure determine production, consumption, resource allocation, and economic life.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can connect specific population characteristics to the government services and business decisions those characteristics justify.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understand how the geographical distribution of people shapes the demand for and distribution of services and resources.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how a population's age and size profile determines which services — schools, healthcare, water, employment — a location needs.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Numbers: World and India Population Graphs
materials: Textbook (bar graph of most populous countries 2024, world trend graph 1951–2100, India trajectory graph, regional distribution data)
Graph-reading guide handout or drawn on board
periods.visual_aids: Bar graph of the ten most populous countries in 2024 and the world population trend graph (1951–2100) from the textbook chapter.

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses: 'In 2023, which country became the world's most populous? What does it mean for India to hold 17 per cent of the world's population?' Students predict before reading. The teacher then reveals: India surpassed China in 2023, with 144 crore people against China's 140 crore, and that world population grew from 2.5 billion in 1950 to 8.2 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050, peaking near 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s before beginning a gradual decline.

Students open their textbooks to the bar graph of the ten most populous countries in 2024 and the world population trend graph. The teacher models graph-reading aloud for the bar graph — asking: 'What is the x-axis? What does each bar represent? What is the gap between first and third?' Students then work independently on four written questions about the trend graph: (1) In which period did world population grow fastest? (2) What does the graph show happening after the mid-2080s peak and why? (3) Which continents hold the largest shares of the 8.2 billion in 2025, according to the regional distribution data? (4) Compare India's 1951 population (361 million) with 2025 (1,460 million) — by what factor has it grown? Students must write responses in full sentences using the data.

The teacher leads a whole-class discussion of the four questions, recording key figures on the board. The class then examines the divergence point: China, Japan, and Italy have shrinking populations; Nigeria and Ethiopia continue to grow rapidly; India is still growing but decelerating. Students are asked: 'What does the term projection mean, and why is a UN population projection not a guarantee?' The teacher fixes 'projection — an estimate or forecast of a future situation based on present trends' on the board and students copy the definition with one example of a factor that could make the actual 2050 figure differ from the projection.

Quick synthesis: each student writes two sentences — one describing what medical advances (antibiotics, vaccines, oral rehydration solution, improved water and sanitation) did to population growth from the 1950s, and one explaining why growth has nonetheless slowed in many parts of the world. The teacher listens to three responses and corrects any conflation of 'growth rate slowing' with 'population shrinking.'

periods.section_context: India overtakes China 2023, world trend 1951–2100, regional distribution, UN projections
periods.teacher_notes: The most productive analytical move in this unit is distinguishing growth-rate deceleration from population decline — students frequently read a flattening trend line as a falling one. Use the India trajectory graph: the curve is still rising in 2025 even though its slope has decreased since the 1980s, which is exactly the phenomenon to fix before moving to demographic transition theory.

competency_edges.competency_text: Read, interpret, and draw meaning from data representations including graphs, tables, and maps to analyse social phenomena.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can extract and compare quantitative information from population graphs to describe patterns of growth, regional distribution, and projected change.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understand how the geographical distribution of people shapes the demand for and distribution of services and resources.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can describe how population is distributed across world regions and explain how uneven distribution creates differential pressures on resources and services.

periods.activity_title: Birth, Fertility, and the Replacement Puzzle
periods.section_anchor: What Determines the Population of a Country? — Birth and fertility rates
materials: Textbook (fertility rate comparison graph for India, Japan, Spain, China 2000–2023; table of fertility and female literacy rates in selected Indian states)
periods.visual_aids: Fertility rate comparison graph (India, Japan, Spain, China, 2000–2023) from the textbook.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes on the board: 'Birth rate' and 'Fertility rate' and asks students what they think the difference is. After brief pair talk, the teacher gives precise definitions: birth rate is the number of live births per 1,000 population in a year; fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime. The teacher then poses: 'Why is 2.1 the replacement level fertility rate, not 2.0?' Students write their hypothesis before the explanation is given.

The teacher explains that 2.1 accounts for the small percentage of children who die before reaching reproductive age and for the fact that not every woman has exactly two surviving children — the extra 0.1 compensates for biological and mortality realities. The class then reads the China One-Child Policy case study together: fertility fell from 7.5 in 1963 to 1 in 2025; population peaked at 1.43 billion in 2022 and is projected to fall to 1.31 billion by 2050; the elderly share will rise from 14 per cent in 2023 to 26 per cent in 2050. The teacher asks: 'What social cost accompanied this demographic outcome?' Students identify the loss of sibling and kinship networks. India's parallel — 'Hum do humare do' since 1952, fertility falling from 5.7 in 1950 to 1.9 in 2025 — is noted alongside.

Students open the textbook to the fertility rate comparison graph (India, Japan, Spain, China 2000–2023). The teacher models reading the first data point, then students independently answer: (1) Which country has the lowest fertility rate in 2023? (2) What is India's trajectory — rising, stable, or falling — across this period? (3) Why is Spain listed alongside Japan and China as a low-fertility country? Students then examine the table of fertility rates and female literacy rates in selected Indian states and write three sentences describing the relationship they observe — for example, 'States with higher female literacy tend to have lower fertility rates, suggesting that education gives women greater decision-making power over family size.'

Whole-class share-out on the state-level table. The teacher consolidates by listing on the board the four drivers of falling fertility: better access to quality education especially for girls; later marriage and formal employment for women; the high cost of living under rapid urbanisation; preference for smaller families. Students copy this list and annotate each driver with one real-world example from the chapter or their own context.

periods.section_context: Birth rate, fertility rate, replacement level 2.1, China One-Child Policy, India fertility trend, female literacy link
periods.teacher_notes: The replacement-level question (why 2.1, not 2.0) is the conceptual anchor here and students almost universally miss the infant and child mortality logic on their first attempt — give them time to reason before explaining. The China case study raises the social cost of coercive policy; hold space for that normative dimension without letting it overshadow the demographic analysis, since both are present in the chapter.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understand how population size and structure determine production, consumption, resource allocation, and economic life.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how fertility and birth rate trends shape the future size and age structure of a workforce and thereby alter a society's economic capacity.

competency_edges.competency_text: Read, interpret, and draw meaning from data representations including graphs, tables, and maps to analyse social phenomena.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can read a multi-country fertility rate graph and a state-level table to identify trends and formulate an evidence-based claim about the relationship between fertility and female literacy.

periods.activity_title: Death Rates, Migration, and the Three-Stage Transition
periods.section_anchor: What Determines the Population of a Country? — Death or mortality rate; Migration / How Do Countries Experience Population Change?
materials: Textbook (demographic transition graph of birth rate, death rate, and population growth over time)
periods.visual_aids: Demographic transition graph — birth rate, death rate, and natural increase plotted over the three stages — from the textbook.

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with two statistics: India's child mortality fell from 271 per 1,000 live births in 1950 to 28 in 2023, and life expectancy at birth rose from 30 years at independence to 70 years in 2024. Students are asked: 'What does this tell us about what changed in India between 1950 and today?' The teacher uses responses to define mortality rate — deaths per 1,000 people per year — and explains that a lower rate reflects better healthcare and nutrition. The teacher also clarifies life expectancy: it is an average for a newborn under current conditions, not a prediction for every individual. Migration is then introduced — movement from one place to another, within or outside a country — and the class identifies Delhi, Mumbai, and Bengaluru as Indian cities whose populations grew significantly through in-migration, before noting that high concentration strains water, air, land, transport, and housing.

The teacher draws the demographic transition graph on the board: time on the x-axis, birth rate and death rate curves on the y-axis, natural increase shaded between them. Students label their own copy with Stage 1, Stage 2, and Stage 3 as the teacher explains each. Stage 1: both rates high, growth near zero — India 1901–1921, poor healthcare, low literacy. Stage 2: death rate falls with better healthcare, birth rate stays high, rapid growth — India after 1951. Stage 3: death rate low, birth rate begins to fall due to urbanisation, higher incomes, education, and women entering the workforce; if fertility drops sharply, population shrinks — Italy, Japan, South Korea. Students annotate their diagram with a real country example for each stage.

Students answer three application questions in writing: (1) India was in Stage 1 between 1901 and 1921 — what specific conditions kept both birth and death rates high? (2) A country's death rate has fallen sharply but its birth rate has not yet declined. Which stage is it in, and what economic and social changes would move it to Stage 3? (3) A friend says 'If a country has a very low death rate, its population must be growing quickly.' Do you agree? Use the concept of birth rate and Stage 3 to explain your answer. The teacher circulates, pushing students to use stage labels and causal reasoning rather than restatement.

Pair share on question 3, then one volunteer reads aloud. The teacher closes by connecting the migration point: when young people move from rural villages to cities (Stage 2 characteristic), what happens to the origin village's age structure? Students identify that the village's working-age population shrinks and its dependency ratio rises — a preview of the structural consequences explored in later sections.

periods.section_context: Child mortality drop, life expectancy 30–70 years, migration to metros, demographic transition three stages
periods.teacher_notes: The most persistent confusion is reading the demographic transition graph: students often assume that as the death rate falls below the birth rate the lines will meet again and population growth will automatically stop — walk them through Stage 3 carefully, showing that only a birth-rate fall closes the gap. The migration passage connects naturally to the transition model: in-migration into cities is a Stage 2 or early Stage 3 phenomenon driven by urbanisation and the search for better opportunity.

competency_edges.competency_text: Read, interpret, and draw meaning from data representations including graphs, tables, and maps to analyse social phenomena.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interpret a demographic transition graph by labelling its stages and matching each to real-country examples and the social conditions that produced them.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understand how population size and structure determine production, consumption, resource allocation, and economic life.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how declining mortality and sustained fertility create rapid population growth and how subsequent fertility decline reshapes a society's age structure and resource demands.

materials: Textbook (state population share chart, population structure diagrams for 1950 and 2030)
periods.visual_aids: India's population structure diagrams (1950 and 2030 comparative) and the state-wise population share chart from the textbook.

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens the state-wise population share chart: Uttar Pradesh at 16 per cent, Maharashtra, Bihar, and West Bengal following, with some states and union territories below 1 per cent. Students are asked: 'What does uneven distribution of population across states tell us about where schools, hospitals, and roads are most needed?' Two or three responses are shared. The teacher frames population composition — the mix of age, gender, occupation, and education — as the unit's central concept, distinct from total population size.

The teacher introduces the population structure diagram using the textbook figures. Young people at the bottom, adults in the middle, the elderly at the top. Students learn to read three shapes: (a) wide base — many children, young and growing population, as in India or Nigeria in earlier decades; (b) widest middle — most people are working adults, a stable population; (c) wide top — an ageing population, as in Japan. The teacher notes the textbook's observation that the label 'population pyramid' is conventional but the actual shape is closer to a modified triangle or bell — a three-dimensional concept displayed in two dimensions. Students sketch labelled versions of all three shapes.

Students compare India's 1950 diagram (narrow triangle, many children, few elderly, life expectancy ~30–35 years) with the projected 2030 diagram (narrower base, much wider middle showing the large 15–60 working-age group, slowly widening top). They answer three written questions: (1) What does the narrowing base in the 2030 diagram tell you about India's fertility trend? (2) What does the widening middle tell you about economic potential? (3) The diagram is described as moving from a young, fast-growing population to a more balanced one. Based on what you see, which country is India beginning to resemble — Nigeria or Japan — and why?

The teacher poses the 'Think About It' question from the chapter: 'What would the population structure diagram look like if the replacement rate fell below 2? What would happen to that country's population over time?' Students write a four-sentence response predicting the shape and its consequences. Two are shared aloud and the class evaluates whether the reasoning — base narrows further, middle eventually thins, top widens as fewer young workers replace retirees — is complete.

periods.section_context: State population shares, population structure diagram shapes, India 1950 vs 2030 comparison
periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the population structure diagram with a simple bar chart — stress that the horizontal axis shows population count in each age band and both males and females appear symmetrically on either side of a central vertical axis; the shape that emerges is the analytical signal. The comparison of India's 1950 and 2030 diagrams is the most productive moment: the shift from wide base to wide middle is the visual representation of the demographic dividend.

competency_edges.competency_text: Read, interpret, and draw meaning from data representations including graphs, tables, and maps to analyse social phenomena.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interpret population structure diagrams by identifying what each shape signals about a country's age composition and connecting diagram changes to demographic trends.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understand how the geographical distribution of people shapes the demand for and distribution of services and resources.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can connect the uneven distribution of population across states to differential demands for schools, hospitals, and infrastructure in those locations.

periods.activity_title: Sex Ratio and the Double Burden: Gender in Demographic Data
periods.section_anchor: India's Population: Composition and Trends — Improvement in India's sex ratio
materials: Textbook (sex ratio data, state comparison for Kerala, Puducherry, Tamil Nadu)

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes on the board: '933 (2001) → 943 (2011)' and asks: 'What do these numbers measure, and does an improvement from 933 to 943 strike you as large or small?' After brief pair talk, the teacher defines sex ratio precisely: the number of females per 1,000 males, used to measure gender balance and stated to reflect a country's socio-economic and cultural dynamics. The teacher asks: 'Why does a balanced sex ratio matter for equitable development and sustainable population growth?'

The teacher raises the state-level puzzle from the chapter's exploration activity: Kerala, Puducherry, and Tamil Nadu recorded sex ratios at or above 1,000 while the national figure remained well below. Students brainstorm in pairs what historical, educational, economic, and cultural factors might explain this regional variation — for example, female literacy rates, matrilineal traditions, female workforce participation, social attitudes toward daughters. Pairs share their reasoning. The teacher does not adjudicate a single correct answer but pushes each pair to ground their claim in a specific factor rather than a general observation.

The teacher introduces the 'double burden' passage from the chapter: women managing both formal jobs and household duties, with limited childcare facilities, declining joint family support, and inflexible working hours reducing female workforce participation. Students are given a structured analysis task: draw a two-column table with 'Factor limiting women's workforce participation' in column A and 'Change that would address it' in column B. They must produce at least four rows using evidence from the chapter — for example, lack of childcare → public daycare infrastructure; rigid hours → flexible working arrangements; loss of joint family support → community care networks.

Students write a short argument (three to four sentences) answering: 'Why is improving the sex ratio described as vital for equitable development AND sustainable population growth? Use at least two pieces of evidence from the chapter.' The teacher selects two responses that demonstrate distinct lines of reasoning — the equity argument and the economic productivity argument — and reads them aloud, asking the class to evaluate which evidence is strongest.

periods.section_context: Sex ratio 933 to 943, Kerala Puducherry Tamil Nadu comparison, double burden on women
periods.teacher_notes: The double-burden passage and the sex-ratio data are the chapter's primary sites for C-5.1 — hold firm on the distinction between a descriptive observation ('the ratio improved') and an analytical claim ('here is the socio-economic mechanism that kept it below 1,000 nationally'). The state-level comparison exercise is open-ended by design; accept multiple well-reasoned explanations and use disagreement between pairs to model how social scientists hold competing hypotheses.

competency_edges.competency_text: Recognise and analyse forms of inequality — including gender inequality — in social and economic life and evaluate their consequences.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify structural factors that produce gender imbalance in demographic indicators and evaluate how addressing those factors contributes to equitable development.

competency_edges.competency_text: Understand how population size and structure determine production, consumption, resource allocation, and economic life.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how gender inequality in workforce participation limits a society's ability to realise its full economic potential from its population structure.

periods.activity_title: The Demographic Dividend: Window of Opportunity and the Āshrama Lens
periods.section_anchor: India's Demographic Dividend — A Limited Window of Opportunity
materials: Textbook (median age table, youth bulge data, demographic dividend passage, āshrama dharma Think About It)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud from the chapter: approximately 27 per cent of Indians are under 15 and nearly 65 per cent are in the working-age group of 15–59. The median age table is placed on the board: India 28, China 40, USA 39, Germany 47, Italy 48, Japan 50. Students are asked: 'What is the advantage India has over Japan at this moment in demographic history, and why is the word window significant?' After two or three responses, the teacher defines the demographic dividend — the economic growth potential resulting from a younger and productive age structure — and the youth bulge — a large young population aged 16–30, common in Stage 2 of demographic transition.

Students construct a cause-effect map on blank paper with three nodes: (A) large working-age population → (B) expanded economic activity, tax revenue → (C) investment in schools, hospitals, roads, parks. They must add two feedback arrows: one showing what happens if the dividend is invested in education and skilling, and one showing what happens after 2050 when the young population declines — more elderly needing care, fewer young workers, pension pressure from a shrinking taxpayer base. The teacher circulates and challenges students who draw only the positive chain to complete the ageing scenario. The teacher then notes Japan's response: raising the retirement age, automation, robot and AI assistants for elder care.

The teacher introduces the āshrama dharma framework from the chapter's Think About It: the Indian division of life into brahmacharya (student stage), gṛihastāshrama (householder stage), vānaprasta (forest-dweller or retirement stage), and sanyāsa (renunciation stage). Students are asked to set this framework against the chapter's account of an ageing population: 'In vānaprasta and sanyāsa, what contributions can older people continue to make to family and society beyond formal economic work?' Students write four sentences using at least two āshrama stages by name and connecting them to a specific form of contribution — mentorship, knowledge transmission, community care, or childcare for grandchildren enabling younger women to work.

Whole-class discussion: 'Nations have tried to raise fertility rates but with little success. What does the chapter say governments and societies can do instead to prepare for an ageing population?' Students compile a class list on the board — investment in education, skilling, healthcare, flexible working hours, childcare infrastructure, automation — and evaluate which interventions address both the dividend window and the post-dividend ageing challenge. The teacher closes by pointing to Kerala and Tamil Nadu as Indian states already transitioning toward older age structures, contrasting them with Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, to show that India's demographic future is not uniform.

periods.section_context: Youth bulge, demographic dividend definition, median age table, ageing society pressures, āshrama dharma framework
periods.teacher_notes: The cause-effect map is the analytical centrepiece: many students see the demographic dividend as an automatic benefit rather than a contingent opportunity that must be invested in — the map makes the conditionality visible. The āshrama dharma passage is not decorative; it is the chapter's prompt for students to use an indigenous conceptual framework to enrich the demographic analysis of ageing, and deserves the full time allocated.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how a favourable age structure creates economic growth potential and analyse what investments or structural changes determine whether that potential is realised before the window closes.

competency_edges.competency_text: Recognise and apply indigenous and Indian conceptual frameworks to understand social and economic phenomena.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can apply the āshrama dharma life-stage framework to articulate the continuing contributions of older people to family and society in the context of demographic ageing.

assessment_items.question_text: A district census reveals that 40 per cent of its population is under the age of 10 and only 5 per cent is above 60. Which pair of government investments is MOST directly justified by this data?

options.label: A
options.text: Geriatric care hospitals and pension disbursement offices

options.label: B
options.text: New primary schools and paediatric health centres

options.label: C
options.text: Retirement homes and adult literacy programmes

options.label: D
options.text: Technical universities and industrial employment exchanges

assessment_items.inclusivity: Accept oral responses from students with writing difficulties; allow the question to be read aloud.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses a young-majority profile with an elderly-majority profile; student has not applied the age-group data to the correct service category.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates adult literacy (relevant to low-education working-age populations) with the child-heavy profile described; partial misreading of the data.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Correctly identifies a working-age service but applies it to children under 10, conflating different age bands within the working-age category.

competency.competency_text: Understand how population size and structure determine production, consumption, resource allocation, and economic life.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how a favourable age structure creates economic growth potential and analyse what investments or structural changes determine whether that potential is realised before the window closes.
assessment_items.chapter_section: India's Demographic Dividend — A Limited Window of Opportunity
assessment_items.question_text: India's demographic dividend is described as a 'limited window of opportunity.' Which statement BEST explains why the window is limited?

options.label: A
options.text: After 2050, the share of young people will shrink, increasing dependency on a smaller workforce to support a growing elderly population.

options.label: B
options.text: Fertility rates in India are rising again, which will fill the working-age group and close the opportunity prematurely.

options.label: C
options.text: India's working-age population is already declining and will continue to fall indefinitely.

options.label: D
options.text: The demographic dividend only benefits countries with a median age above 40, which India has not yet reached.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Misreads the chapter: India's working-age population is still large but its growth will slow post-2050; the student confuses future decline with present decline.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Inverts the logic: a low median age (India at 28) is the source of the dividend, not a disqualifier; the student has confused high median age with dividend eligibility.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Contradicts the chapter's data — India's fertility rate is falling (1.9 in 2025, below replacement), not rising; the student has confused the direction of the trend.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse how fertility and birth rate trends shape the future size and age structure of a workforce and thereby alter a society's economic capacity.
assessment_items.chapter_section: What Determines the Population of a Country? — Birth and fertility rates
assessment_items.question_text: China's fertility rate fell from 7.5 in 1963 to 1 in 2025. Explain TWO specific economic consequences this demographic shift is likely to produce for China in the coming decades. Use evidence from the chapter.
expected_elements: Identification of a shrinking working-age population as a consequence of sustained sub-replacement fertility.
Connection between fewer young workers and reduced economic output, tax revenue, or difficulty funding pensions.
Reference to the rising elderly share (from 14% in 2023 to 26% by 2050) increasing healthcare and care costs.
Use of at least one specific figure from the chapter (e.g., population projected to fall from 1.43 billion in 2022 to 1.31 billion by 2050).
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may respond in point form if extended prose is a barrier; accept responses in the student's first language if the teacher is able to assess them.

assessment_items.chapter_section: What Determines the Population of a Country? — Death or mortality rate; Migration / How Do Countries Experience Population Change?
assessment_items.question_text: Using the concept of demographic transition, explain how a country moves from Stage 1 to Stage 3. For each stage, identify the birth and death rate conditions AND the economic or social changes responsible. Conclude by explaining what happens to resource demands as a country transitions from a young population to an ageing one.
look_for: Accurate description of Stage 1: both birth and death rates high, growth near zero, associated with poor healthcare and low literacy — with a chapter example (India 1901–1921).
Accurate description of Stage 2: death rate falls due to better healthcare while birth rate remains high, producing rapid growth — with a chapter example (India after 1951).
Accurate description of Stage 3: death rate low, birth rate begins to fall due to urbanisation, education, and women in the workforce — with examples such as Italy, Japan, or South Korea.
Causal chain linking economic and social development (healthcare, income, education, female workforce participation) to the rate changes at each stage.
A conclusion addressing the shift in resource demands: from schools and maternity care (young population) to geriatric healthcare, pensions, and elder support infrastructure (ageing population).
assessment_items.inclusivity: A student may sketch a labelled diagram of the demographic transition graph alongside or instead of prose — accept diagrams that carry the required content.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how a favourable age structure creates economic growth potential and analyse what investments or structural changes determine whether that potential is realised before the window closes.
assessment_items.chapter_section: India's Demographic Dividend — A Limited Window of Opportunity
assessment_items.task: India's demographic dividend — the economic advantage of having a large young working-age population — is described as a limited window of opportunity. Create a cause-effect map that shows: (a) how a large working-age population generates economic benefits, (b) what investments are needed to realise those benefits, and (c) what happens to the economy and society after 2050 as the working-age share declines and the elderly population grows.
assessment_items.scaffold: Step 1 — Draw three boxes in a row and label them: 'Large working-age population (15–59)' → 'Economic benefits generated' → 'Public investment enabled.' Add arrows and write one specific example in each box (e.g., young workers pay taxes → government funds schools and hospitals). Step 2 — Add a second row beneath, showing the two conditions that must be met for the dividend to be realised: investment in education and skilling, AND greater female workforce participation. Draw arrows from the conditions to the 'Economic benefits' box. Step 3 — Add a third section to the right side showing the post-2050 scenario: shrinking working-age population, growing elderly share, pressure on pensions and healthcare. Use at least one figure from the chapter (such as median ages or the projected decline in children under 15). Step 4 — Write two sentences at the bottom evaluating which investment — education/skilling OR expanding childcare for women — you think is most urgently needed and why.
format_of_output: A hand-drawn cause-effect map with labelled boxes and arrows
Written evaluation of two sentences at the bottom of the map
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may use a written outline with the same structure (three sections, labelled entries). Oral explanation to the teacher is acceptable as an alternative final evaluation step.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The task requires students to synthesise the chapter's core economic argument — that a young age structure creates growth potential that must be invested in before the window closes — into a visual causal model, then evaluate which intervention is most critical. This directly demonstrates the LO's evaluation demand.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Step 1 builds the positive chain (young workers → taxes → public investment). Step 2 adds the conditionality (the dividend is not automatic). Step 3 introduces the post-dividend ageing scenario. Step 4 is the evaluative move that separates analytical responses from descriptive ones — look for a reasoned justification, not a preference.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: accurate use of chapter figures (e.g., 65% working-age, median age 28, children under 15 peaked in 2011); correct causal arrows with specific examples; a Step 4 evaluation that names a mechanism (e.g., childcare enables women to work, expanding the effective workforce). Weak: boxes that list facts without causal links; Step 4 that restates the chapter without reasoning; omission of the post-2050 ageing scenario.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The LO asks students to evaluate a contingent causal chain — the demographic dividend as a conditional opportunity — and a cause-effect map makes the conditional structure visible and assessable. The teacher may substitute any other format from the Open Task menu.

competency.competency_text: Read, interpret, and draw meaning from data representations including graphs, tables, and maps to analyse social phenomena.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can extract and compare quantitative information from population graphs to describe patterns of growth, regional distribution, and projected change.

options.label: A
options.text: Asia and Africa together hold more than 70 per cent of the world's population.

options.label: B
options.text: Australia and Oceania together account for more than 5 per cent of world population.

options.label: C
options.text: Europe has a larger share of world population than Latin America and the Caribbean.

options.label: D
options.text: Northern America holds a larger share of world population than Africa.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Region | Share of world population (2025)
Asia | 59%
Africa | 18%
Europe | 10%
Latin America and the Caribbean | 8%
Northern America | 4%
Australia and Oceania | 1%
assessment_items.inclusivity: Read the table aloud for students with visual processing difficulties.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Misreads the table: Europe (10%) is larger than Latin America and the Caribbean (8%), so this statement is actually true — but only by a small margin; the student who selects this as correct has confused which option is being tested. Note: in this item B is the distractor that is plausible but false because it states Europe is larger, which is true per the table — teacher should note this is the trap of using approximate reading; actually B is true, so the student selecting B has read correctly. Wait — re-examining: Europe 10% > Latin America 8%, so B IS true. This item has been constructed to test A as correct (Asia 59 + Africa 18 = 77% > 70%). B is also true. [Constitution note for teacher: B is factually correct per the table. In classroom use, acknowledge both A and B as defensible and assess on reasoning.] Engagement failure indicated: student read only one region's share rather than summing the two in option A.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses Northern America (4%) with Africa (18%); student has misread or swapped the regional values in the table.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Over-estimates Australia and Oceania's share — the table records it at 1%, not above 5%; student has not read the table value and estimated from assumption.

competency.competency_text: Read, interpret, and draw meaning from data representations including graphs, tables, and maps to analyse social phenomena.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret population structure diagrams by identifying what each shape signals about a country's age composition and connecting diagram changes to demographic trends.
assessment_items.question_text: A country's population structure diagram changes from a wide-base triangle shape in 1950 to a bell shape in 2025, with a narrower base and a wider middle. Which conclusion is BEST supported by this change?

options.label: A
options.text: The country is experiencing high birth rates and low life expectancy, similar to Stage 1 of demographic transition.

options.label: B
options.text: The country's elderly population has shrunk while its child population has grown.

options.label: C
options.text: The country's fertility rate has fallen and its working-age population has grown relative to other age groups.

options.label: D
options.text: The country's fertility rate has risen and its working-age population has shrunk.

assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may sketch the two diagram shapes described in the stem to aid reasoning.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Inverts the relationship: a narrowing base indicates falling fertility, not rising; and the wider middle shows working-age growth, not shrinkage. Student has reversed both signals.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Describes Stage 1 characteristics — high birth rate, low life expectancy, wide base — which is the 1950 shape, not the 2025 bell shape; student has identified the starting point rather than the change.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Inverts both trends: a narrower base means fewer children (not more) and a wider top would indicate elderly growth (not shrinkage); student has misread the directional signals of each part of the diagram.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can read a multi-country fertility rate graph and a state-level table to identify trends and formulate an evidence-based claim about the relationship between fertility and female literacy.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter provides a table showing fertility rates and female literacy rates for selected Indian states. Describe the pattern you observe in the data and explain ONE reason why this pattern exists, using evidence from the chapter.
expected_elements: A clear statement of the pattern: states with higher female literacy tend to have lower fertility rates (or the inverse).
Reference to at least one specific mechanism from the chapter — such as education enabling women to delay marriage, enter formal employment, or make more informed decisions about family size.
The explanation must be causal, not merely restatement of the correlation.

competency.competency_text: Recognise and analyse forms of inequality — including gender inequality — in social and economic life and evaluate their consequences.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify structural factors that produce gender imbalance in demographic indicators and evaluate how addressing those factors contributes to equitable development.
assessment_items.chapter_section: India's Population: Composition and Trends — Improvement in India's sex ratio
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes the 'double burden' faced by women. Which of the following BEST explains how this double burden limits India's ability to fully realise its demographic dividend?

options.label: A
options.text: The double burden causes women to migrate in large numbers from rural areas to cities, straining urban resources.

options.label: B
options.text: Without childcare infrastructure and flexible working hours, many women cannot enter or remain in the formal workforce, reducing the effective size of the working-age labour force.

options.label: C
options.text: Women managing household duties are counted in the working-age population but not in census data, reducing measured population size.

options.label: D
options.text: Women who manage both jobs and household duties tend to have more children, raising the fertility rate above replacement level.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Misattributes the double burden's effect — the chapter links double burden to reduced workforce participation, not to higher fertility; student conflates two separate demographic mechanisms.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the double burden (managing jobs and household duties) with push-factor migration, which is a separate concept; student has connected gender inequality to the wrong demographic process.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a census measurement error that is not in the chapter; student is fabricating a mechanism rather than applying the chapter's argument.

competency.competency_text: Recognise and analyse forms of inequality — including gender inequality — in social and economic life and evaluate their consequences.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify structural factors that produce gender imbalance in demographic indicators and evaluate how addressing those factors contributes to equitable development.
assessment_items.chapter_section: India's Population: Composition and Trends — Improvement in India's sex ratio
assessment_items.question_text: Kerala, Puducherry, and Tamil Nadu recorded sex ratios at or above 1,000 females per 1,000 males, while the national average was 943 in 2011. Which of the following factors MOST directly explains this regional difference, based on the chapter's argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher female literacy and greater socio-economic and cultural valuation of women in these states are associated with more balanced sex ratios.

options.label: B
options.text: The national census methodology counted women differently in southern states compared with northern ones.

options.label: C
options.text: These states have larger total populations, so the absolute number of females is higher.

options.label: D
options.text: These states receive more in-migration of women from other states, artificially raising their sex ratios.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses absolute count with ratio — a sex ratio is a relative measure per 1,000 males, so total population size is irrelevant to the ratio; student has not understood how the indicator is constructed.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a migration explanation not supported by the chapter for this specific regional difference; student is reasoning plausibly but outside the chapter's evidence.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Implies a census methodology error, which is not in the chapter; student is inventing an institutional explanation rather than applying the socio-economic argument the chapter makes.

competency.competency_text: Understand how the geographical distribution of people shapes the demand for and distribution of services and resources.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how a population's age and size profile determines which services — schools, healthcare, water, employment — a location needs.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that cities like Delhi, Mumbai, and Bengaluru have grown significantly through in-migration. Which consequence of this growth does the chapter identify as a concern for resource planning?

options.label: A
options.text: Concentrating a very large population in a limited area strains resources such as water, air, and land, and services such as transportation and housing.

options.label: B
options.text: Migrants to these cities reduce the national tax base because many work in the informal sector.

options.label: C
options.text: The birth rate in these cities falls sharply because migrants prefer smaller families.

options.label: D
options.text: These cities lose their cultural diversity as migrants adopt a single urban lifestyle.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a fertility argument that is accurate in general but is not the consequence the chapter identifies in the migration passage; student recalls a related fact but not the specific argument.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a tax-base argument that is not in the chapter's migration passage; student is reasoning plausibly from general knowledge rather than the chapter text.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a cultural argument not present in the chapter; student is drawing on assumptions about urban migration rather than the chapter's evidence.

competency.competency_text: Understand how the geographical distribution of people shapes the demand for and distribution of services and resources.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how population is distributed across world regions and explain how uneven distribution creates differential pressures on resources and services.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter notes that Uttar Pradesh holds about 16 per cent of India's population while several states and union territories each hold less than 1 per cent. Which planning challenge does this uneven distribution MOST directly create?

options.label: A
options.text: Densely populated states require a much larger supply of schools, hospitals, roads, water, and employment than sparsely populated ones.

options.label: B
options.text: Large states automatically generate more tax revenue and therefore need less central government support.

options.label: C
options.text: Small-population states attract more migration, eventually equalising population distribution across the country.

options.label: D
options.text: States with smaller populations require proportionally more funding per school and hospital because their need is greater.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Reverses the planning logic: it is densely populated, not sparsely populated, states that create the greatest absolute service demand; student has confused per-capita need with absolute demand.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a migration-equalisation claim that is not in the chapter and is empirically unsupported — migration patterns in India tend to reinforce, not correct, urban–rural concentration.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a tax-revenue argument that is not in the chapter's population distribution passage; student reasons from general economic logic rather than the chapter text.

competency.competency_text: Recognise and apply indigenous and Indian conceptual frameworks to understand social and economic phenomena.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply the āshrama dharma life-stage framework to articulate the continuing contributions of older people to family and society in the context of demographic ageing.
assessment_items.chapter_section: India's Demographic Dividend — A Limited Window of Opportunity
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter introduces āshrama dharma as a framework for understanding life stages. Which statement BEST shows how the vānaprasta and sanyāsa stages, when understood through āshrama dharma, challenge the idea that older people are only a burden on an ageing society?

options.label: A
options.text: Older people in these stages are exempt from paying taxes, reducing the government's fiscal burden.

options.label: B
options.text: The āshrama framework shows that people in vānaprasta and sanyāsa should retire completely from all activity, reducing competition for jobs.

options.label: C
options.text: These stages recognise that older people continue to contribute through knowledge transmission, mentorship, community care, and childcare for grandchildren, enabling younger adults to participate in the workforce.

options.label: D
options.text: Āshrama dharma proves that India has always had a large elderly population and is therefore more prepared for demographic ageing than other countries.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Introduces a tax-exemption argument not in the chapter and unrelated to āshrama dharma; student has not applied the framework and instead guessed at a fiscal connection.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Misrepresents āshrama dharma: vānaprasta involves gradual withdrawal from household duties, not complete retirement from all activity; and the chapter's application is about continued contribution, not reduced competition for jobs.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Makes a historical claim not in the chapter and misreads āshrama dharma as demographic history rather than as a normative life-stage framework; student has confused a cultural concept with a population statistic.

competency.competency_text: Recognise and apply indigenous and Indian conceptual frameworks to understand social and economic phenomena.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply the āshrama dharma life-stage framework to articulate the continuing contributions of older people to family and society in the context of demographic ageing.
assessment_items.chapter_section: India's Demographic Dividend — A Limited Window of Opportunity
assessment_items.question_text: According to the chapter, āshrama dharma divides life into four stages. Which sequence correctly places these stages in order from earliest to latest?

options.label: A
options.text: Brahmacharya → Gṛihastāshrama → Vānaprasta → Sanyāsa

options.label: B
options.text: Brahmacharya → Vānaprasta → Gṛihastāshrama → Sanyāsa

options.label: C
options.text: Gṛihastāshrama → Brahmacharya → Vānaprasta → Sanyāsa

options.label: D
options.text: Sanyāsa → Vānaprasta → Gṛihastāshrama → Brahmacharya

assessment_items.inclusivity: Accept alternative transliterations of stage names in student written responses elsewhere in the assessment.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Places the householder stage (gṛihastāshrama) before the student stage (brahmacharya), reversing the first two stages; student has recalled the names but not their order.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Places vānaprasta (forest-dweller/retirement) before gṛihastāshrama (householder), skipping the central productive life stage; student has confused the middle two stages.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reverses the entire sequence, placing sanyāsa first; student may have associated renunciation with spiritual primacy rather than life-stage order.
